abstract: |
  Consistency among Sentinel-2 processing levels is essential when normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) time series combine top-of-atmosphere (TOA) and surface-reflectance (SR) products. We quantified paired NDVI differences among Level-1C/TOA, Sen2Cor L2A/SR, and LaSRC L2A/SR for 106 land-use management polygons on 22 farms in the Colombian Orinoco Piedmont. Acquisitions from 2019-2020 were matched by date and polygon. Local L1C and LaSRC observations were screened with Fmask 4.6 and s2cloudless, and Sen2Cor observations with the Scene Classification Layer. Across 1,797 common observations, mean differences were +0.116 for LaSRC-L1C (95% farm-cluster bootstrap CI, 0.108 to 0.124; RMSD = 0.121; CCC = 0.653; Deming slope = 1.092; 95% limits of agreement, 0.047 to 0.184) and +0.095 for Sen2Cor-L1C (0.086 to 0.101; RMSD = 0.101; CCC = 0.743; slope = 1.155; limits, 0.027 to 0.162). LaSRC and Sen2Cor agreed more closely (mean difference = +0.021; RMSD = 0.036; CCC = 0.962; slope = 0.945, CI 0.916 to 0.972; limits, -0.035 to 0.078), with nearly identical mean differences in 2019 and 2020. TOA-SR differences were largest for secondary forest or wetlands undergoing restoration and smallest for other agricultural practices. On 2,585 paired records, masking changed neither the mean difference (+0.0001; CI, -0.0021 to 0.0024) nor CCC (+0.0014; -0.0078 to 0.0146) distinguishably from zero, but increased the Deming slope by +0.0191 (0.0028 to 0.0312). Sentinel-2 NDVI differences were therefore processor- and land-use-dependent, supporting explicit harmonization when TOA and SR observations are combined.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Radiometric consistency is fundamental to the interpretation of vegetation-index time series derived from Sentinel-2 MSI [@Drusch2012]. Conversion from Level-1C top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance to Level-2A surface reflectance (SR) changes the red and near-infrared signals used to calculate NDVI because atmospheric correction responds to aerosol optical thickness, water vapour, illumination-view geometry, and surface spectral properties [@Doxani2018; @Martins2017; @Marujo2021]. These effects are particularly relevant in humid tropical environments, where persistent cloud, cirrus, and high atmospheric water vapour complicate the construction of radiometrically consistent multi-year series [@Chraibi2022].

Sen2Cor and LaSRC are two established routes for generating Sentinel-2 SR products. Sen2Cor is the European Space Agency Level-2A processor distributed through the Copernicus ecosystem [@MainKnorn2017; @ESA2026Sen2Cor]. LaSRC was developed for Landsat and subsequently adapted for Sentinel-2; it is also the atmospheric-correction component used in the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 workflow [@Vermote2016; @Vermote2018; @Claverie2018]. Previous intercomparisons have evaluated atmospheric-correction products over forests, inland waters, and AERONET sites [@Martins2017; @Marujo2021; @Chraibi2022], but evidence remains limited for heterogeneous tropical landscapes in which pastures, trees, restoration areas, and agricultural uses coexist within short distances.

This study addresses processor-associated NDVI differences in a spatially clustered network of land-use management polygons in the Piedemonte Orinocense transition zone, with three specific objectives for the complete 2019-2020 observation period: (i) to quantify the magnitude and structure of paired NDVI differences among L1C/TOA, Sen2Cor L2A/SR, and LaSRC L2A/SR; (ii) to characterize how these differences vary across the six Sustainable Cattle Ranching (SCR) land-use categories represented in the analytical sample; and (iii) to evaluate how Fmask+s2cloudless screening of LaSRC observations affects paired agreement with SCL-screened Sen2Cor observations.

The study quantifies agreement and processor-associated differences rather than absolute accuracy, because no co-located field or atmospheric reference was available to identify which product was closest to true surface NDVI.

# Study Area and Data {#sec-area}

## Study Area {#sec-study-area}

The area of interest is located in the Colombian Orinoco Piedmont (*Piedemonte Orinocense*), Department of Meta, Colombia, an ecological and biogeographic transition belt between the eastern foothills of the Cordillera Oriental and the Llanos Orientales plains. It comprises 22 farms with a combined mapped area of 854 ha across Granada, Fuente de Oro, San Juan de Arama, and El Castillo (@fig-study-area). For these farms, the 2019 vector inventory contains 143 management-polygon features, which together cover the mapped farm area and define 141 management polygons identified by farm, polygon, and land-use code; these polygons constitute the spatial units of analysis. The farms intersect the adjacent Sentinel-2 MGRS tiles 18NXJ and 18NXK in UTM zone 18N. <!-- [VERIFY V14] The IDEAM ecosystem and land-cover percentages below were computed on the earlier 91-polygon set; recompute them on the 143 features (or the 106 analytical polygons) before submission. --> Overlay of the management polygons with the IDEAM continental ecosystems map [@IDEAM2017Ecosistemas] shows that polygon area is dominated by the Alternating-Hygric Tropical Zonobiome (*Zonobioma Alternohígrico Tropical*; 66.3%), with smaller contributions from the Humid Tropical Zonobiome (13.7%) and the Subandean Orobiome (9.5%). Consistent with a long-transformed silvopastoral landscape rather than an open-savanna setting, the IDEAM 2020 land-cover layer [@IDEAM2020Coberturas] classifies only 0.5% of polygon area as natural grassland, while 66.6% corresponds to managed pasture and 7.9% to forest cover. All valid acquisitions matched across the processing pipelines during 2019 and 2020 were included, without restriction to a seasonal or phenological window.

The polygon inventory was produced within the Sustainable Cattle Ranching project (SCR; *Proyecto Ganadería Colombiana Sostenible*), an institutional partnership involving FEDEGÁN-FNG, CIPAV, Fondo Acción, The Nature Conservancy, and the World Bank [@SCROperationalManual2014; @SCR2019Inventory].

## SCR Land-Use Categories {#sec-ut}

Land-use codes follow the official SCR land-use manual [@SCRLandUseManual2017]. The category-stratified analysis included the six categories represented in the common three-pipeline dataset (@tbl-ut); English translations are used throughout the results and discussion, and original Spanish category labels are omitted here for brevity.

| Code | Land-use category |
|:---:|---|
| UT2 | Secondary forest or wetlands undergoing restoration |
| UT3 | Scattered trees in pasture and vegetative succession |
| UT4 | Agroforestry crops |
| UT6 | Agricultural land with vegetation cover greater than 80% |
| UT7 | Intensive silvopastoral system |
| UT8 | Other agricultural practices |

: Official SCR land-use categories represented in the analysis [@SCRLandUseManual2017]. {#tbl-ut}

## Analytical Dataset {#sec-inclusion}

The observational unit was a polygon-by-date record. The polygon identifier combined the farm identifier, the polygon number, and the SCR land-use code. A record entered the three-pipeline comparison when the same acquisition date and polygon identifier were present for L1C, Sen2Cor, and LaSRC, and when the locally processed L1C and LaSRC observations each contained at least 10 valid 10 m pixels after Fmask+s2cloudless screening. Polygon-by-date records that remained duplicated within a pipeline, because two inventory features shared the same identifier, were excluded rather than averaged. Exact matching yielded 1,810 records; one record was removed during cross-product quality control (@sec-statistics), and 12 records failed the valid-pixel threshold in the LaSRC pipeline. The common three-pipeline dataset therefore comprised 1,797 polygon-by-date records from 106 management polygons on 22 farms (668 records in 2019 and 1,129 in 2020).

The land-use analysis comprised the 1,527 common records from 88 management polygons on 21 farms assigned to the six SCR categories in @tbl-ut. The masking-sensitivity analysis used the 2,585 polygon-by-date records (128 polygons, 20 farms) present in both the masked and unmasked LaSRC exports and paired with the same SCL-screened Sen2Cor observations; a stricter subset of 2,521 records with at least 10 valid pixels in both LaSRC exports was analysed as a sensitivity check.

## Processing Pipelines {#sec-processing}

The comparison held acquisition date, polygon identifier, B8/B4 NDVI formulation, and a 10 m target resolution constant across the three pipelines. Atmospheric correction, pixel-quality screening, processing platform, and zonal-aggregation implementation differed among pipelines and are therefore part of the processing-chain effect evaluated in this study.

**L1C/TOA pipeline.** Sentinel-2 Level-1C images for tiles 18NXJ and 18NXK were retrieved from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem with EODAG 3.10.2. Scenes were pre-screened using `CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE <= 20`. For products with Processing Baseline 04.00 or later, the 1000-DN offset was removed before reflectance scaling, thereby maintaining consistency with harmonized Sentinel-2 collections [@GEE2026S2SR]. NDVI was calculated from B8 (near infrared, 10 m) and B4 (red, 10 m).

**Sen2Cor L2A/SR pipeline.** Sen2Cor-derived SR was obtained from `COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED` through the Google Earth Engine Python API for acquisitions between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2020. The collection harmonizes digital-number ranges across Sentinel-2 processing baselines [@GEE2026S2SR]. For each target date of the local inventory, the least cloudy image within a short search window was selected; all 175 selected images coincided exactly with the target acquisition date. Because the archive does not expose a local executable version for each image, the results refer to the harmonized collection rather than to a single locally executed Sen2Cor release. Zonal statistics were calculated on the native B8 projection at 10 m.

**LaSRC L2A/SR pipeline.** The corresponding L1C acquisitions were processed with `sen2lasrc` v2.0.2, which executes LaSRC 3.2.0 and integrates EODAG, Fmask, and s2cloudless in a Docker workflow [@deBoissieu2024; @Qiu2019; @SentinelHubS2Cloudless]. The processing image was the `lasrc-fmask` image of the `sen2lasrc` project, pinned by its SHA-256 digest (`14fcc58ac2bd…`; the full digest is recorded in `environment/container-provenance.txt` of the Zenodo deposit; see the Data Availability Statement). MODIS-based fused atmospheric auxiliary data (MODIS_FUSED) for 2019-2020 were retrieved through the USGS Machine-to-Machine (M2M) API [@USGS2026M2M]. Surface reflectance was stored as scaled `INT16`; pixels assigned the product no-data value were removed before NDVI calculation.

## Cloud and Shadow Screening {#sec-masks}

Sen2Cor observations were screened with the Scene Classification Layer (SCL). Classes 1 (saturated or defective), 3 (cloud shadow), 8 and 9 (medium- and high-probability cloud), 10 (thin cirrus), and 11 (snow or ice) were excluded; pixels without valid reflectance (class 0, no data) carry no valid B4 or B8 values in the Earth Engine collection and therefore did not contribute to the zonal statistics. The local L1C and LaSRC pipelines shared the same pixel mask: Fmask 4.6 and s2cloudless layers were generated once by `sen2lasrc` at 20 m, resampled to the 10 m analysis grid, and applied identically to both pipelines, retaining pixels classified as clear land by Fmask and as cloud-free by s2cloudless. The only masking asymmetry in the three-pipeline comparison was therefore between this shared mask and the Sen2Cor SCL screening. Consequently, the observed inter-pipeline differences combine the effects of atmospheric correction with residual differences in masking, rasterization, and zonal aggregation. The paired masking analysis isolates the effect of LaSRC screening on a fixed set of polygon-by-date observations.

## Angular and BRDF Considerations {#sec-angular}

No normalization to a common bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) geometry was applied, although Sentinel-2 reflectance shows measurable directional effects across the swath [@Roy2017]. LaSRC atmospheric correction is distinct from the NBAR/BRDF normalization subsequently applied in the HLS product [@Franch2019; @Ju2025HLS; @USGSHLS2024]. Solar zenith angles in the archived L1C metadata were approximately 25-38 degrees and view zenith angles approximately 0-9 degrees; residual illumination-view effects may therefore contribute to the observed differences.

## NDVI Calculation and Zonal Aggregation {#sec-aggregation}

NDVI was calculated pixel-wise as

$$
\mathrm{NDVI}=\frac{\rho_{B8}-\rho_{B4}}{\rho_{B8}+\rho_{B4}}.
$$

For each polygon-by-date record, mean NDVI was the primary statistic; median, standard deviation, and valid-pixel count were retained for quality control. Local L1C and LaSRC statistics were calculated with `rasterio.mask`. Sen2Cor statistics were calculated with Google Earth Engine `reduceRegions` using the native B8 projection and a 10 m scale.

## Pairwise Differences {#sec-differences}

Pairwise differences were defined as

$$
\Delta\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{LaSRC-L1C}}=\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{LaSRC}}-\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{L1C}},
$$

$$
\Delta\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{Sen2Cor-L1C}}=\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{Sen2Cor}}-\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{L1C}},
$$

and

$$
\Delta\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{LaSRC-Sen2Cor}}=\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{LaSRC}}-\mathrm{NDVI}_{\mathrm{Sen2Cor}}.
$$

Positive values indicate higher NDVI in the first-named pipeline.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-statistics}

Agreement was evaluated using the mean paired difference, root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), unbiased RMSD (uRMSD), Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), Deming regression, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement [@Lin1989; @Linnet1993; @BlandAltman1986]. The mean paired difference measures the systematic shift between pipelines, RMSD measures total pairwise deviation, and uRMSD measures the residual deviation after removal of the mean shift. CCC evaluates agreement relative to the 1:1 line by combining precision and accuracy components. Deming regression was fitted with $\lambda=1$, representing equal error-variance contributions from the two compared pipelines because independent pipeline-specific measurement-error variances were unavailable. Bland-Altman limits of agreement were calculated as the mean paired difference $\pm 1.96$ standard deviations of the paired differences. The coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of the paired values is reported descriptively and was not used as a measure of agreement. All statistics were calculated for 2019, for 2020, and for the pooled 2019-2020 dataset.

Repeated dates within polygons, and polygons within farms, violate the independence assumption of a record-level bootstrap. Therefore, 95% confidence intervals for the mean difference, CCC, and Deming slope, for the paired masking contrasts, and for the category-specific estimates were obtained with a farm-cluster bootstrap: farms were resampled with replacement and all polygons and dates of each selected farm were retained [@DavisonHinkley1997]. Each analysis used 2,000 replicates with a fixed random seed (2026) and percentile intervals (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles). A 95% interval excluding zero (or one, for Deming slopes) was interpreted as evidence that the corresponding contrast was statistically distinguishable from that value. Category estimates based on fewer than five farms were interpreted descriptively because the number of independent resampling units was limited.

One polygon-by-date record (farm 442, polygon P7, 21 December 2020) was removed during cross-product quality control. Its Sen2Cor NDVI was 0.066, compared with 0.333 for L1C and 0.468 for LaSRC. The removal was data-dependent rather than based on a pre-specified threshold and is therefore considered when interpreting the results.

## Three-Pipeline Agreement {#sec-three-pipeline-agreement}

The common dataset contained 1,797 polygon-by-date observations from 106 polygons on 22 farms. Both SR pipelines produced systematically higher NDVI than L1C (@tbl-agreement-3vias; @fig-agreement-3vias). The LaSRC-L1C mean difference was +0.116 (95% CI, 0.108 to 0.124), with RMSD = 0.121 and uRMSD = 0.035; the Sen2Cor-L1C mean difference was +0.095 (0.086 to 0.101), with RMSD = 0.101 and uRMSD = 0.034. In both comparisons, the mean shift accounted for most of the total deviation, and the estimated Bland-Altman limits of agreement were entirely above zero. The Deming slopes of 1.092 (1.050 to 1.122) and 1.155 (1.120 to 1.179) exceeded one, indicating that neither TOA-SR relationship can be represented by a constant additive shift alone.

![Agreement diagnostics for the common 2019-2020 dataset. Rows compare LaSRC-L1C, Sen2Cor-L1C, and LaSRC-Sen2Cor. Left panels show Deming regression and the 1:1 line; right panels show Bland-Altman difference-versus-mean diagnostics.](figures/figure_04_agreement_diagnostics.pdf){#fig-agreement-3vias fig-align="center" width="94%" fig-pos="htbp"}

Agreement between the two SR pipelines was substantially stronger than agreement between either SR pipeline and L1C. LaSRC-Sen2Cor had a mean difference of +0.021, RMSD = 0.036, uRMSD = 0.029, and CCC = 0.962. The Deming slope of 0.945, whose confidence interval (0.916 to 0.972) excluded one, and the intercept of +0.059 indicate a small proportional component, while the limits of agreement [-0.035, +0.078] show that individual differences may occur in either direction. Thus, Sen2Cor and LaSRC were closely concordant but not numerically interchangeable.

The same pattern was observed separately in each year (@tbl-agreement-annual). The LaSRC-Sen2Cor mean difference was practically identical in 2019 (+0.021) and 2020 (+0.021), with overlapping confidence intervals, and its Deming slope was below one in both years. The TOA-SR mean differences were slightly larger in 2019 than in 2020, and CCC was lower in 2020 for all three comparisons. For LaSRC-L1C in 2019, the Deming slope interval (0.996 to 1.084) included one, so a proportional component was not distinguishable for that year alone.

## Sensitivity to LaSRC Masking {#sec-masking-sensitivity}

Masking sensitivity was evaluated on the identical set of 2,585 observations (128 polygons, 20 farms) available in both LaSRC exports (@tbl-mask-paired). The masked-minus-unmasked change in mean difference was +0.0001 (95% farm-cluster bootstrap CI, -0.0021 to 0.0024), and the change in CCC was +0.0014 (-0.0078 to 0.0146). Both intervals included zero. The Deming slope increased by +0.0191 (0.0028 to 0.0312), whose interval excluded zero, indicating a small but statistically distinguishable change in the proportional relationship. Restricting the comparison to the 2,521 records with at least 10 valid pixels in both LaSRC exports gave the same conclusions: +0.0002 (-0.0021 to 0.0026) for the mean difference, +0.0019 (-0.0079 to 0.0160) for CCC, and +0.0179 (0.0017 to 0.0297) for the Deming slope.

| Metric | Masked LaSRC | Unmasked LaSRC | Difference (masked-unmasked) | 95% farm-cluster bootstrap CI |
|:------------------|---------:|---------:|----------:|------------------:|
| Mean difference relative to Sen2Cor | +0.020 | +0.020 | +0.0001 | [-0.0021, +0.0024] |
| CCC | 0.954 | 0.953 | +0.0014 | [-0.0078, +0.0146] |
| Deming slope | 0.950 | 0.931 | +0.0191 | [+0.0028, +0.0312] |

: Paired masking comparison on 2,585 common polygon-by-date observations (128 polygons; 20 farms). {#tbl-mask-paired}

These results indicate that Fmask+s2cloudless screening did not materially change the aggregate mean difference or concordance for observations retained in both datasets, although it produced a small change in the Deming slope.

## Differences among SCR Land-Use Categories {#sec-gradiente-ut}

The category-stratified dataset comprised 1,527 observations from 88 polygons on 21 farms. Mean paired differences were positive in every category and for all three comparisons (@tbl-gradiente-ut; @fig-gradiente-ut). For LaSRC-L1C, category means ranged from +0.095 in UT8 to +0.139 in UT2. For Sen2Cor-L1C, they ranged from +0.076 in UT8 to +0.126 in UT2. The corresponding 95% farm-cluster bootstrap intervals for UT2 and UT8 did not overlap in either TOA-SR comparison. Because a direct UT2-UT8 contrast was not estimated and some categories were represented by only two to four farms, the pattern is interpreted as category-associated variation rather than as a formal pairwise hypothesis test.

The LaSRC-Sen2Cor differences were smaller and varied over a narrower range (+0.009 to +0.027) than either TOA-SR comparison. Their ordering across categories differed from the TOA-SR pattern, indicating that land-use dependence was not identical for all three processor pairs.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Inter-Processor Agreement {#sec-disc-agreement}

The two atmospheric-correction pipelines changed NDVI in the same general direction relative to L1C, but the magnitude and proportional structure differed. The positive mean differences and positive Bland-Altman limits for LaSRC-L1C and Sen2Cor-L1C show that SR-derived NDVI was consistently higher than TOA-derived NDVI in this dataset. The low uRMSD relative to RMSD indicates that systematic displacement, rather than random pairwise dispersion, accounted for most of the TOA-SR disagreement. Nevertheless, Deming slopes above one demonstrate an NDVI-dependent component, so a single additive adjustment would not reproduce either SR series across the observed range.

Sen2Cor and LaSRC showed high concordance (CCC = 0.962) and a much smaller mean difference and RMSD than either comparison with L1C. This close agreement is consistent with both processors removing a substantial common atmospheric component. However, the Deming slope of 0.945, non-zero intercept, and limits of agreement spanning negative and positive values show that the two SR products are not equivalent at the polygon-by-date level. The near-identical LaSRC-Sen2Cor mean difference in 2019 and 2020, together with Deming slopes below one in both years, suggests that this residual offset was stable over the study period rather than driven by a single year.

The residual LaSRC-Sen2Cor differences cannot be assigned to a single algorithmic source. Plausible contributors include the atmospheric auxiliary data, aerosol and water-vapour retrievals, radiative-transfer parameterization, cloud-screening implementation, rasterization, and observation geometry [@MainKnorn2017; @Vermote2016; @Vermote2018]. Because the LaSRC output analysed here was not an HLS NBAR product, BRDF normalization is not attributed to LaSRC itself [@Franch2019; @USGSHLS2024].

## Land-Use Dependence {#sec-disc-gradiente}

The largest TOA-SR differences occurred in UT2, which comprises secondary forest or wetlands undergoing restoration, whereas the smallest occurred in UT8, which comprises other agricultural practices. This pattern is consistent with land-use-dependent differences in canopy structure, shadow fraction, and red and near-infrared spectral response. However, these mechanisms were not isolated experimentally, and the limited number of farms in UT2, UT4, and UT7 constrains the precision of category-level inference.

The narrower and differently ordered LaSRC-Sen2Cor differences indicate that much of the category-associated TOA-SR pattern was common to both atmospheric-correction pipelines. The remaining SR-SR variation was comparatively small and should be interpreted as a residual processor effect rather than as evidence of a uniform category correction.

## Masking Sensitivity {#sec-disc-masking}

On the paired observation set, Fmask+s2cloudless screening produced no statistically distinguishable change in the aggregate mean difference or CCC, because both cluster-bootstrap intervals included zero. The small increase in Deming slope was statistically distinguishable from zero, indicating that screening modified the proportional relationship more than the average offset. In this analysis, masking therefore operated primarily as pixel-quality selection rather than as a direct radiometric adjustment of the retained polygon means.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

First, the farms form a spatially clustered observational sample within one tropical landscape, so the numerical estimates should not be generalized without independent replication. Second, the absence of co-located field spectroradiometry or atmospheric reference measurements prevents assessment of absolute processor accuracy. Third, the Sen2Cor and local pipelines used different cloud-screening and aggregation environments, so the processing-chain effect cannot be attributed exclusively to atmospheric correction. Fourth, no explicit BRDF normalization was applied. Fifth, one observation was removed through data-dependent quality control; a pre-specified exclusion rule would provide stronger protection against analytical discretion. Sixth, the farm-cluster bootstrap preserves dependence among dates and among polygons within farms, but no explicit hierarchical model was fitted, and several land-use categories are represented by few farms. Seventh, records of two inventory features that shared the same polygon identifier, and polygon-by-date records duplicated within a pipeline, were excluded rather than reconciled. Finally, the Earth Engine notebook used for the final Sen2Cor export was not preserved; the SCL screening rule is therefore documented from an earlier version of the extraction code and from the structure of the exported records.

## Implications for Multi-Year NDVI Analysis {#sec-outlook}

Sentinel-2 time series that combine L1C and SR observations should not assume that the products differ only by a constant offset. Harmonization should account for both systematic and proportional differences and should be validated within the target landscape and land-use composition. Future comparisons should apply a common pixel mask and grid to locally processed outputs, fit hierarchical models of dates, polygons, and farms, include an external atmospheric or surface reference, and evaluate additional years and independent tropical landscapes.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

Across 1,797 common polygon-by-date observations from 106 management polygons on 22 farms in 2019 and 2020, LaSRC and Sen2Cor produced higher NDVI than L1C by mean paired differences of +0.116 and +0.095, respectively. The corresponding Deming slopes of 1.092 and 1.155 show that these differences contained both systematic and proportional components.

Agreement between the SR products was markedly stronger (mean difference = +0.021; RMSD = 0.036; CCC = 0.962), and the mean difference was stable between years, although the Deming slope of 0.945 and limits of agreement from -0.035 to +0.078 show that Sen2Cor and LaSRC were not interchangeable for individual polygon-date observations.

The TOA-SR differences varied among SCR land-use categories, with the largest values in secondary forest or wetlands undergoing restoration and the smallest in other agricultural practices. On the paired masking subset, the mean difference and CCC were statistically stable, whereas the Deming slope changed slightly. These findings support explicit, locally validated harmonization when Sentinel-2 NDVI series combine TOA and SR products or multiple atmospheric-correction processors.
